findings.title: BCB Resolution 561 – Stablecoin Cross-Border Remittance Ban in Force; VASP Authorisation Deadline 30 October 2026
findings.summary: BCB Resolution 561 (effective 1 October 2026) prohibits payment firms from settling cross-border remittances in crypto assets, including dollar-pegged stablecoins. In addition, existing VASPs must apply for BCB authorisation by 30 October 2026; after that date, regulated banks and financial institutions may not service unauthorised crypto companies.
findings.client_impact: Brazilian-resident clients or clients with Brazilian business operations who use stablecoin rails for cross-border transfers must transition to alternative remittance channels immediately, as such transfers became unlawful on 1 October. Any client exposed to a Brazilian VASP (exchange, crypto payment processor) must verify that the VASP has or has applied for BCB authorisation before 30 October, or risk losing banking services for that counterparty.
findings.urgency_reason: Two concurrent deadlines: the stablecoin ban is already in force (immediate compliance needed), and the VASP authorisation deadline of 30 October 2026 falls within 25 days – squarely within the URGENT 30-day window. Failure to act could result in disruption to client payment flows and loss of banking access for VASP counterparties.
findings.source_name: FCM Law – Brazil VASP Licence: BCB Rules, Deadlines and FAQ (2026)

findings.title: Supplementary Law 227/2026 – ITCMD Now Levied on Overseas Assets at Market Value
findings.summary: Supplementary Law No. 227/2026 (in force January 2026) requires mandatory market-value assessment of inherited or gifted assets in Brazil and extends ITCMD (inheritance and gift tax) jurisdiction to overseas assets where the beneficiary is Brazilian. Tax jurisdiction is determined by the nature and location of assets.
findings.client_impact: HNW Brazilian clients with overseas trusts, foreign real estate, or offshore investment portfolios now face potential ITCMD exposure on those assets when transferred to Brazilian beneficiaries – a fundamental change that did not previously exist. Existing estate plans built on the assumption that offshore assets were beyond ITCMD scope should be reviewed and likely restructured.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH rather than URGENT because the law came into force in January 2026 and there is no imminent filing deadline; however, the structural impact on ongoing estate and succession planning is severe and clients with Brazilian beneficiaries should be engaged without delay.
findings.source_name: Chambers Private Wealth 2026 – Brazil

findings.title: AMLA Publishes Three Final Draft RTS on CDD and AML Cooperation Standards – Binding ~January 2027
findings.summary: On 1 October 2026, AMLA published three final draft RTS covering customer due diligence measures, triggers, and supervisory cooperation. The standards apply six months after publication in the EU Official Journal; with the current parliamentary review timeline, binding law is expected by approximately January 2027.
findings.client_impact: Clients holding accounts, structures, or operating companies in Luxembourg, Cyprus, or Malta can expect enhanced CDD obligations and more prescriptive onboarding triggers at their EU-regulated financial institutions within the next three to four months, potentially requiring updated source-of-wealth documentation and ownership chain disclosures.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the standards are not yet binding (currently in Commission/Parliament review), but the three-month horizon to binding effect makes proactive client preparation advisable now rather than at implementation.
findings.source_name: AMLR Explained – Didit / AMLA regulatory timeline

findings.title: Beneficial Ownership Transparency Act 2026 – Expanded Scope to Private Funds and Trusts
findings.summary: The Beneficial Ownership Transparency Act 2026 expanded disclosure requirements to private funds, mutual funds, and trust structures, lowered reporting thresholds, and introduced a 'legitimate interest' access model (not fully public). Access requires a demonstrated legitimate interest and payment of increased search fees.
findings.client_impact: Clients with Cayman Islands private funds, mutual funds, or trust structures that were previously outside beneficial ownership registration requirements are now in scope and must file disclosure information with the Cayman registry; failure to comply risks deregistration as CIMA accelerates enforcement ahead of its 2027 FATF evaluation.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the Act is already enacted and the immediate filing obligations are in effect; clients not yet assessed for compliance under the expanded scope should be reviewed urgently, though no single 30-day deadline triggers URGENT status.
findings.source_name: Global Law Experts – Cayman Islands Beneficial Ownership Reforms 2026

findings.title: CIMA Entity Removals at Record High – 443 Deregistrations YTD; Annual Return Fee Raised 28%
findings.summary: CIMA removed 443 entities from its register through early October 2026 (up 54% from 2025), reflecting aggressive housekeeping ahead of the Caribbean FATF evaluation in December 2027. The Fund Annual Return filing fee increased approximately 28% from CI$350 to CI$450 per fund per year.
findings.client_impact: Clients with dormant or under-active Cayman vehicles face elevated deregistration risk as CIMA increases scrutiny; the annual compliance cost for active funds has risen, and clients should confirm all fund vehicles are current on filings and fees to avoid involuntary removal from the register.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because there is no single imminent deadline, but the pace of removals signals that non-compliant or administratively lapsed entities face a meaningfully higher risk of forced deregistration in the near term.
findings.source_name: Cayman Compass – CIMA removals hit record high in 2026

findings.title: BVI Beneficial Ownership Register – Legitimate Interest Access Open; Threshold Lowered to 10%
findings.summary: From 1 April 2026, the BVI Registry accepts legitimate interest applications to access beneficial ownership records. The threshold for disclosure as a beneficial owner was lowered from 25% to 10%, significantly expanding the universe of individuals who must be registered.
findings.client_impact: Clients with BVI companies where minority shareholders or controllers hold between 10% and 25% must now be registered as beneficial owners – a category that was previously exempt – and those individuals' names and interests may be accessible to parties demonstrating legitimate interest, increasing transparency risk for clients who relied on the prior 25% threshold for privacy.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the changes are already in force (April 2026); clients who have not yet reviewed and updated their BVI beneficial ownership filings under the 10% threshold should do so promptly, as non-compliance leaves structures exposed during any third-party access request.
findings.source_name: Harneys – BVI Beneficial Ownership Information Updates

findings.title: Luxembourg 2026 Budget – Carried Interest Exemption, SPF Reform, and Start-up Tax Credit
findings.summary: For tax year 2026, Luxembourg introduced a carried interest tax exemption for AIF participations held more than six months representing no more than 10% of fund share capital, authorised SPFs to be established as simplified joint-stock companies, and introduced a 20% income tax credit (capped at €100,000 per investor per year) on investments of at least €10,000 in eligible start-ups.
findings.client_impact: Fund managers and general partners with Luxembourg AIF structures can now structure eligible carried interest with a tax exemption, potentially reducing effective tax rates on performance fees significantly; HNW investors in Luxembourg SPFs benefit from a more flexible corporate form, while angel/early-stage investors in eligible start-ups can claim meaningful tax credits against Luxembourg income.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because these measures are already operative for the 2026 tax year; clients with Luxembourg structures should review whether they can restructure carried interest arrangements or SPF forms to take advantage of the new regime before year-end 2026.
findings.source_name: Ogier – Luxembourg Tax Update: What's New in 2026

findings.title: Panama Decree 25/2026 – FATCA/CRS Controlling Person Threshold Reduced from 25% to 10%
findings.summary: Panama's Ministry of Economy and Finance reduced the ownership/control threshold for reportable controlling persons under FATCA and CRS from 25% to 10% via Decree No. 25 (June 2026). Reporting institutions may rely on AML/KYC procedures to treat trust settlors and foundation founders as controlling persons. SBP Rule 1-2026 also added enhanced BOI requirements for FinTech entities.
findings.client_impact: Clients with Panama foundations, trusts, or corporate vehicles where individuals control 10%–25% of the structure now fall into the reportable controlling person category under both FATCA and CRS, meaning their tax residency information will be reported to relevant foreign tax authorities – a significant expansion of automatic tax information exchange exposure for Panama-based wealth structures.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the decree came into force in June 2026 and the first reporting cycle under the new threshold will arrive; clients with Panama structures should verify whether any new controlling persons need to be captured in the next reporting cycle before the annual deadline.
findings.source_name: KPMG Tax News Flash – Panama: Ownership Threshold Reduced under FATCA and CRS

findings.title: MAS Circular AMLD 05/2026 – Risk-Proportionate Source of Wealth Guidance for Wealth Management
findings.summary: On 25 May 2026, MAS issued Circular AMLD 05/2026 with operational guidance for private banks, family offices, and asset managers on establishing source of wealth (SOW) in a risk-proportionate manner, operationalising Singapore's updated AML framework effective January 2026.
findings.client_impact: HNW clients banking or investing through Singapore-regulated entities can expect more structured and evidence-based SOW reviews at onboarding and periodic review, with risk-proportionate escalation for higher-risk clients; clients with complex business histories or multi-jurisdictional wealth origins should prepare comprehensive and updated SOW documentation to avoid account delays.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the circular is already in force and Singapore-based financial institutions are actively implementing the guidance; clients with Singapore accounts or family office structures should ensure their SOW files are current and aligned with the risk-proportionate framework to avoid remediation requests.
findings.source_name: Alpadis – MAS Source of Wealth Guidance

findings.title: FINMA Consults on Revised AML Ordinance – Targets Complex Corporate Structure Transparency Before 2027 FATF Evaluation
findings.summary: FINMA launched a consultation on 12 May 2026 on a partially revised AML Ordinance. Proposed new rules would require financial intermediaries to identify the natural person behind every complex corporate structure. Separately, the UK-Switzerland Berne Financial Services Agreement (BFSA) entered into force 1 January 2026, facilitating cross-border private banking.
findings.client_impact: HNW clients with multi-layer or complex corporate structures held at Swiss private banks should anticipate enhanced UBO look-through requirements once the revised Ordinance enters into force; the UK-BFSA opening also creates new opportunities for UK-connected clients to access Swiss private banking services with reduced regulatory friction.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the consultation is ongoing and binding rules have not yet been issued; however, the 2027 FATF evaluation creates a firm implementation horizon and clients with Swiss accounts should begin preparing updated UBO documentation for complex structures.
findings.source_name: FinCrime Central – Swiss Regulator FINMA Updates AML Standards for 2026

findings.title: OECD Pillar Two – 2026 Administrative Guidance on UTPR Safe Harbour and Side-by-Side Arrangements
findings.summary: The OECD issued May 2026 administrative guidance covering late-filing penalty treatment for jurisdictions that implemented the Global Minimum Tax from 2024, transitional UTPR Safe Harbour updates for 52–53-week fiscal years, and core elements of a new Side-by-Side arrangement with safe harbours for MNEs headquartered in eligible-regime jurisdictions.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients who own or partially control multinational enterprises operating in Pillar Two jurisdictions should review whether the Side-by-Side safe harbour arrangements reduce their effective GloBE liability and whether their structures qualify for the transitional UTPR Safe Harbour, which could affect the net tax cost of holding operating companies in certain jurisdictions.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the guidance is technical and applies to MNEs in scope of Pillar Two; there is no single imminent deadline, but the ongoing evolution of administrative guidance makes this a continuing review item for clients with qualifying multinational structures.
findings.source_name: Deloitte – OECD Pillar Two Global Minimum Tax

findings.title: UAE Onshore Change-of-Control Notification/Clearance Regime Established (2026)
findings.summary: UAE onshore legislation enacted in 2026 established a new regime requiring prior notification or regulatory clearance for changes of control in onshore licensed financial entities, aligning with pre-existing DIFC and ADGM rules.
findings.client_impact: HNW clients contemplating mergers, acquisitions, or ownership restructurings involving UAE-regulated wealth management firms or financial institutions must now plan for a regulatory notification or clearance process before completing any change of control, which could add weeks or months to deal timelines and require disclosure of the ultimate controlling party.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the regime is already operative in 2026; clients considering any UAE-regulated financial entity transactions should build regulatory clearance into their deal timelines now to avoid unexpected delays.
findings.source_name: Mondaq – UAE Change of Control Rules for Regulated Financial Businesses

findings.title: Cyprus FDI Screening Law in Effect from 2 April 2026 – Low Thresholds and Look-Back Provisions
findings.summary: Cyprus's Foreign Direct Investment Screening Law came into force on 2 April 2026, introducing notification requirements with relatively low thresholds, look-back provisions for prior transactions, and defined internal trigger points for ownership changes in Cypriot entities.
findings.client_impact: Foreign clients acquiring or restructuring interests in Cyprus-based entities – including holding companies, real estate vehicles, and operational businesses – must assess whether the transaction meets the notification threshold and, if so, seek pre-clearance; the look-back provisions mean that transactions completed prior to 2 April may also warrant review for notification obligations.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the law is already in force and the look-back provisions create retrospective risk; clients with pending or recent Cyprus transactions should confirm compliance status with local counsel before the screening authority initiates its own review.
findings.source_name: White & Case – Foreign Direct Investment Reviews 2026

findings.title: FinCEN Final Rule – BOI Reporting Permanently Eliminated for US Domestic Companies (August 2026)
findings.summary: Effective 14 August 2026, FinCEN permanently removed BOI reporting requirements under the Corporate Transparency Act for all US domestic companies and US persons. Previously filed BOI for US persons will be deleted. Foreign companies registered to do business in the US remain subject to BOI requirements.
findings.client_impact: US-domiciled clients operating through US domestic entities no longer have any BOI filing obligations and need not maintain or update prior submissions; however, clients who use foreign entities registered in the US (e.g., BVI or Cayman vehicles registered as foreign reporting companies) must continue to meet BOI requirements and should confirm compliance status.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because the rule is already in force and the primary effect is relief from a prior obligation; no new action is required for domestic entities, though advisors should verify the status of any foreign reporting company registrations on a client-by-client basis.
findings.source_name: Mayer Brown – FinCEN Permanently Eliminates BOI Reporting for US Companies

findings.title: Florida SB 264 – Foreign Buyer Real Estate Restrictions Upheld; Affidavit Requirement Ongoing
findings.summary: Florida SB 264, restricting real estate purchases by foreign principals from seven 'countries of concern' (China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, Syria, Venezuela/Maduro regime), was upheld by courts in November 2025. All buyers must sign compliance affidavits at closing. Chinese-connected buyers face the broadest restrictions on any Florida real property.
findings.client_impact: Clients with connections to any of the seven designated countries must ensure full SB 264 compliance at every Florida property closing, including accurate affidavit completion; violations carry property forfeiture and felony charges, so any client with potential country-of-concern links should be reviewed prior to executing a Florida real estate transaction.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because the law is settled (court-upheld), no new deadlines are approaching, and the requirement is ongoing background compliance; advisors should include SB 264 screening as a standing step in the Florida real estate onboarding workflow.
findings.source_name: South Florida Law PLLC – Foreign Real Estate Buyer Restrictions in Florida

findings.title: FIRPTA – 15% Withholding Rate Applies to Foreign Sellers of US Real Property in 2026
findings.summary: FIRPTA withholding for foreign sellers of US real property remains at 15% in 2026 (10% for personal residences with a sale price not exceeding $1 million). Final regulations under Section 892 governing foreign government investment were released December 2025. The FIRPTA exemption for domestically controlled REITs is fully operative.
findings.client_impact: Foreign clients selling US real property must factor the 15% FIRPTA withholding rate into their transaction planning and liquidity, as the withheld amount is applied to the purchase price, not the gain; buyers bear the withholding obligation, and clients with REIT investments should confirm the domestically controlled exemption applies to their specific holding to avoid unnecessary over-withholding.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because the 15% rate is established and stable in 2026 with no legislative changes pending; this is ongoing awareness for any client transacting in US real property.
findings.source_name: Home Abroad Inc – FIRPTA Guide: Foreign Investors in US Property

findings.title: CRS BRS Version 3.0.0-17 Applicable from 1 March 2026 – New AEOI Data Fields
findings.summary: Technical standard BRS Version 3.0.0-17 for AEOI (CRS/FATCA) became applicable from 1 March 2026, adding new data fields including equity interest type, self-certification, account number type, account type, due diligence procedure, joint account indicators, and controlling person type. The UK separately expanded CRS scope to include electronic money institutions.
findings.client_impact: Clients with accounts at CRS/FATCA-reporting institutions will find that their financial institution's annual information exchange submissions now include more granular data fields, potentially increasing the quality of information that tax authorities receive about account types and beneficial ownership; clients should be aware that the standard for self-certification and due diligence documentation has also been updated.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because this is a technical reporting standard change already implemented by financial institutions; no client action is required, but it signals that AEOI reporting is becoming increasingly granular across jurisdictions.
findings.source_name: SARS – Automatic Exchange of Information BRS AEOI: CRS & FATCA

findings.title: ADGM FSRA Fund Framework Amendments – In Effect from 16 September 2026
findings.summary: ADGM FSRA enacted amendments to its funds framework on 16 September 2026, following consultation paper No. 12 of 2025. The DFSA also recently closed its own funds regime overhaul consultation.
findings.client_impact: Clients with ADGM-domiciled funds or SPVs should review the updated framework to ensure fund documentation and operating procedures reflect the new rules; the parallel DFSA consultation signals that both UAE international financial centre fund regimes are being modernised and further changes at DIFC may follow.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because the ADGM amendments are already in force and represent incremental enhancements rather than a fundamental change; no immediate client action is flagged pending review of specific fund structures against the updated rules.
findings.source_name: Akin Gump – Recent Changes to ADGM and DIFC Funds Framework

findings.title: Jersey Prospectus Requirements Updated – Registrar Consent No Longer Required for International Circulation
findings.summary: The Companies (General Provisions) (Jersey) Amendment Order 2026 and Companies Law (Jersey) Amendment Order 2026 (in force 30 September 2026) remove the Registrar consent requirement for circulating prospectuses outside Jersey, reducing administrative friction for Jersey-domiciled vehicles targeting international investors.
findings.client_impact: Clients using Jersey-domiciled funds or vehicles for international capital raises will benefit from reduced administrative steps and faster time-to-market for prospectus circulation across jurisdictions, making Jersey structures more operationally competitive as an offshore fund domicile.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because the change is already in force and represents a simplification rather than a new compliance obligation; advisors should note this as a positive development when recommending Jersey structures for international capital-raise mandates.
findings.source_name: Jersey Finance – Jersey Moves to Simplify its Financial Services Framework

findings.title: Jersey COBO Amendment Order 2026 – International Capital Raise Controls Largely Eliminated
findings.summary: The Control of Borrowing (Jersey) Amendment Order 2026 removes COBO consent requirements for shares, securities, and ownership interests issued by Jersey entities and certain non-Jersey entities raising money or registering interests in Jersey (subject to States Assembly approval), substantially streamlining Jersey's regulatory framework for fund domiciliation.
findings.client_impact: Clients considering Jersey as a domicile for fund structures or capital market vehicles will face fewer regulatory consent hurdles for international offerings, reducing deal costs and timelines; once States Assembly approval is confirmed, COBO consent for international capital raises will largely cease to be a planning consideration.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because the amendment is pending final States Assembly approval and does not yet impose any compliance obligation; advisors should track final enactment to update Jersey fund domicile recommendations accordingly.
findings.source_name: Appleby – Streamlining of Regulatory Scope in Jersey: COBO Amendment Order 2026

findings.title: Guernsey GFSC – Lending, Credit and Finance Amendment Rules 2026 in Effect; VASP Licence Duplication Removed
findings.summary: Guernsey's Lending, Credit and Finance (Amendment) Rules 2026 came into effect 1 October 2026. GFSC-licensed firms may now undertake virtual asset activity without a separate VASP licence in qualifying circumstances, reducing regulatory duplication for established Guernsey financial service providers.
findings.client_impact: Clients using Guernsey-regulated fund administrators or financial service providers that also engage with digital/virtual assets will benefit from reduced licensing friction and potentially lower compliance costs for their Guernsey-based service providers, though clients' own obligations are unaffected.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because the change benefits Guernsey-domiciled service providers rather than directly imposing obligations on HNW clients; relevant background for clients evaluating Guernsey-based structures with any digital asset exposure.
findings.source_name: Mourant - Guernsey FinReg Quarterly Update Q3 2026

findings.title: Isle of Man – Financial Services (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill Consultation Open
findings.summary: The IOMFSA is consulting on a package of amendments to modernise financial services legislation covering enforcement, civil penalties, warning notices, appeal rights, inspection powers, fees, and regulatory consistency. The Isle of Man is also collaborating with Jersey and Guernsey on a joint Crown Dependencies APP fraud prevention framework.
findings.client_impact: Clients with Isle of Man structures should be aware that the IOMFSA is strengthening its enforcement toolkit and penalty regime, which could increase the consequences of administrative non-compliance; the APP fraud prevention collaboration with Jersey and Guernsey also signals a coordinated uplift in Crown Dependencies AML standards.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because this is a consultation at an early stage with no binding rules yet in effect; advisors with Isle of Man structures should monitor the outcome and flag potential enhanced enforcement implications for clients with existing IoM vehicles.
findings.source_name: Isle of Man Government – Financial Services (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill Consultation
